Question: Amy, Beth, and Jo listen to four different songs and discuss which ones they like. No song is liked by all three. Furthermore, for each of the three pairs of the girls, there is at least one song liked by those two girls but disliked by the third. In how many different ways is this possible?
Solution:
For each song, record exactly which girls like it. The three required pair patterns are Amy and Beth only, Amy and Jo only, and Beth and Jo only. These patterns must each appear at least once, so at least three of the four songs are liked by exactly two girls.

There are two possible cases.

If exactly three songs are liked by pairs, each required pair pattern appears once. Choose the remaining song in \(4\) ways. It can be liked by nobody or by just Amy, Beth, or Jo, giving \(4\) possibilities. Assign the three pair patterns to the other three distinct songs in \(3\cdot2\cdot1=6\) ways. This gives
\[
4\cdot4\cdot6=96
\]
assignments. Each is counted once because its non-pair song and all four patterns are determined.

If all four songs are liked by pairs, one pair pattern appears twice and the other two appear once each. Choose the repeated pattern in \(3\) ways. Choose its two songs in \(4\cdot3/2=6\) ways, dividing by \(2\) because the order of those two songs does not matter. Assign the two remaining patterns to the remaining songs in \(2\) ways. This gives
\[
3\cdot6\cdot2=36
\]
assignments. Here the repeated pattern and its two songs are uniquely determined, so there is no duplication.

These cases exhaust the possibilities and cannot overlap. Therefore the total is
\[
96+36=\boxed{132},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
